extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; scientists and graduate students interested in research practice and the concept of paradigms
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and descriptive standards for recognizing, evaluating, and conducting 'normal science' under the Kuhnian paradigm model: when a paradigm exists, what normal scientific work consists of, how it is communicated, and what kinds of experimental and theoretical problems it produces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm as criterion that a field is a science
rubrics_metrics.description: A field has achieved the status of a science when it has 'achieved a paradigm that proved able to guide the whole group's research.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: astronomy in antiquity, post-1740 electricians (Cavendish, Coulomb, Volta). The possession of a paradigm that practitioners can take for granted is identified as 'hard to find another criterion that so clearly proclaims a field a science.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional communication assumes shared paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: In mature sciences, research is usually reported as brief articles addressed only to professional colleagues who can be assumed to share the paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast earlier stages when books addressed a wider learned world. The shift from books to specialized articles signals professionalization and a widening gulf between specialists and lay readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal science as actualization of paradigm's promise
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal science consists in actualizing a paradigm's initial promise by (a) extending knowledge of facts the paradigm displays as revealing, (b) increasing the match between those facts and the paradigm's predictions, and (c) further articulation/specification of the paradigm itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'mop-up' work is the bulk of scientists' careers; it is not aimed at inventing new theories but at extending, sharpening, and applying the paradigm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three normal foci for factual investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual scientific investigation under a paradigm ordinarily concentrates on three classes of facts: (1) those the paradigm has shown to be particularly revealing, (2) facts that can be directly compared with paradigm predictions, and (3) facts sought to articulate and resolve ambiguities in the paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples for (1): stellar positions, specific gravities, combining weights; for (2): tests like parallax telescopes, Atwood's machine, neutrino detectors; for (3): determination of constants (gravitational constant, Avogadro's number) and experiments to choose among alternative applications of a paradigm (caloric theory examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm-dependence of experimental design and apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: The design and invention of special apparatus and experimental techniques are often motivated and shaped by the paradigm's problems and the sort of facts it makes significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synchrotrons, radiotelescopes, Cavendish apparatus, Atwood's machine, Foucault's apparatus, and neutrino detectors illustrate that experimental ingenuity and resources are applied where a paradigm assures the importance of the sought facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical normal work: application and confrontation with experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal theoretical tasks include using existing theory to produce predictions of intrinsic value and manipulating theory so its applications can be confronted directly with experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: manufacture of ephemerides, lens computations, radio propagation curves, and theoretical manipulations intended to increase precision of applications or to exhibit new applications of the paradigm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms begin limited in scope and precision
rubrics_metrics.description: At first appearance paradigms are often limited both in scope and precision; their apparent success is a promise discoverable in selected and still incomplete examples rather than universal mastery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition of this limited initial scope explains why normal science aims to extend and articulate the paradigm rather than assume it fully adequate from the start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm articulation as combined theoretical and experimental work
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems of paradigm articulation are simultaneously theoretical and experimental: experiments may be designed using theoretical assumptions, and those experiments in turn refine the theory, producing a more precise paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Coulomb needed theory to design his apparatus; his measurements refined theory. Reformulations (Euler, Lagrange, Hamilton, Jacobi) aimed to make the paradigm more coherent and applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal science as puzzle-solving with narrow expected outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal research problems function like puzzles: they rarely aim at major novelties; the expected range of outcomes is small, and results outside that narrow range are typically judged failures of the research rather than revelations about nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This narrow latitude of expectation is built into normal science: experiments are designed to fit the paradigm; anomalies are not ordinarily sought for their own sake during normal research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relaxation mechanism when paradigm fails
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal science contains a built-in mechanism that ensures the relaxation of its restrictive problem-bounds whenever the paradigm ceases to function effectively, at which point scientists begin to behave differently and the nature of problems changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This process sets the stage for scientific revolutions: deserting the paradigm is how revolutions occur, but such desertions are rare and typically follow the advance of normal research and accumulation of anomalies.
